conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode. Helpers: range(n) = high[n]-low[n]; body(n) = close[n]-open[n]; avgRange(N) = average of range over the N bars ending at bar 1; tick = instrument minimum price move (structural constant); highest(x,N)[k] / lowest(x,N)[k] = extreme over N bars ending at bar k; X[n] means the named primitive/candidate X evaluated with all its bar offsets shifted back n additional bars.

candidates.name: TrendBar
candidates.quote: if the bar is a strong bull trend bar, traders will buy at the market as soon as the bar closes
candidates.description: Primitive: bar 0 is a trend bar, closing in the direction of its body with a body that is most of its range.
candidates.pseudocode: close[0] > open[0] && (close[0] - open[0]) >= bodyFraction * (high[0] - low[0])

complexity.reason: single-bar arithmetic on open/high/low/close

notes: Chapter-local primitive; the same shape is defined independently in T07-02 (chapter 7). Dedup pass should merge.

candidates.name: StrongTrendBar
candidates.quote: A very important signal bar is a strong trend bar, especially during the spike phase of a trend.
candidates.description: Primitive: bar 0 is a trend bar with an unusually large body fraction and a range at or above a multiple of the recent average range -- Brooks's 'strong' trend bar.
candidates.pseudocode: TrendBar[0] && (close[0] - open[0]) >= strongBodyFraction * (high[0] - low[0]) && (high[0] - low[0]) >= rangeMultiple * avgRange(rangeLookback)

complexity.reason: adds an average-range window to the trivial trend-bar test

notes: Brooks gives no numeric threshold for 'strong'; the two multipliers are a reading of the text.

candidates.name: TrendSpikeContext
candidates.quote: This urgency results in a series of bull trend bars and an increasingly larger bull spike.
candidates.description: Primitive context filter approximating a trend 'spike': the last spikeBars bars are (almost) all trend bars in the same direction with limited overlap between consecutive bars. Reused with different spikeBars values as a short-window spike proxy or a longer-window 'established trend' proxy elsewhere in this file.
candidates.pseudocode: for k in 0..spikeBars-1: TrendBar[k] (same direction) && (min(high[k],high[k+1]) - max(low[k],low[k+1])) <= maxOverlapFraction * min(range(k),range(k+1)) -> spikeHolds; filter passes when spikeHolds

complexity.reason: identifying a 'spike' or an 'established trend' is a design decision; a run of low-overlap trend bars is one workable proxy

notes: Same proxy family as T07-08 StrongTrendContext, defined independently per the one-primitive-per-chapter rule.

candidates.name: StrongTrendBarCloseEntry
candidates.quote: One common approach is to wait for a bar to close and if the bar is a strong bull trend bar, traders will buy at the market as soon as the bar closes.
candidates.description: Enter with the trend at the close of a strong trend bar occurring during a trend spike.
candidates.pseudocode: StrongTrendBar[0] && TrendSpikeContext[0]
candidates.book_order_type: market order (or an aggressive limit at the close price) placed immediately once the bar closes; other traders use a stop one tick beyond the bar's high/low instead -- both mechanize to next-bar-open here

complexity.reason: inherits the spike-identification design decision from TrendSpikeContext

candidates.name: TwoBarReversal
candidates.quote: A long setup is a bear trend bar immediately followed by a bull trend bar, and a bear setup is a bull trend bar immediately followed by a bear trend bar.
candidates.description: Primitive: two consecutive trend bars of opposite direction and roughly the same size where the pair substantially overlaps -- 'every reversal is a type of two-bar reversal.' Long form: bear trend bar then bull trend bar.
candidates.pseudocode: TrendBar[1] (bear) && TrendBar[0] (bull) && (min(high[0],high[1]) - max(low[0],low[1])) >= overlapFraction * min(range(0),range(1)) && body(0) >= bodySizeRatioMin * body(1) && body(0) <= bodySizeRatioMax * body(1)

complexity.reason: a two-bar shape test with an overlap ratio and a size-similarity ratio

notes: 'About the same size' has no book number; the ratio band is a reading of the text.
Brooks explicitly allows the pair to be non-consecutive bars on the chart's own timeframe in some passages; this primitive covers only the strict consecutive-bar case.

candidates.name: TwoBarReversalEntry
candidates.quote: When two bars overlap so much, the chances of a profitable trade are greater if you short below the lower of the two bars and not below the other.
candidates.description: Enter beyond the combined extreme of the two-bar reversal pair (not just the signal bar) when the pair overlaps heavily.
candidates.pseudocode: TwoBarReversal[0]
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop one tick above max(high[0], high[1]) -- beyond both bars when they overlap heavily, otherwise one tick above the signal bar (bar 0) alone is an acceptable simplification

complexity.reason: inherits TwoBarReversal's two-bar shape test

notes: The stop-beyond-both-bars nuance vs. stop-beyond-signal-bar-only is a risk-placement detail the engine's fixed stop/target inputs do not currently model; recorded in book_order_type.

candidates.name: TwoBarReversalContinuationFade
candidates.quote: In contrast, if the identical two-bar pattern formed in a bull trend at the end of a two-legged pullback to the moving average, this is a two-bar reversal and a good setup for a buy setup... Instead, you should view the bull bar as a one-bar bear flag and consider shorting below it.
candidates.description: When a two-bar reversal forms AGAINST an established strong trend, Brooks treats the countertrend bar as a one-bar flag and fades it -- i.e., continues with the prior trend -- rather than trading the reversal itself. Long form: an established bull trend (context ending just before the pair) is followed by a bull-bar-then-bear-bar reversal pair; buy back above the bear bar's high instead of shorting below it.
candidates.pseudocode: TrendSpikeContext[2] (bull, spikeBars = establishedTrendBars) && TrendBar[1] (bull) && TrendBar[0] (bear) && (min(high[0],high[1]) - max(low[0],low[1])) >= overlapFraction * min(range(0),range(1))
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop one tick above high[0], treating the bear bar as a one-bar bull flag

complexity.reason: requires the same trend-strength judgment as TrendSpikeContext, applied to decide whether to trade WITH the reversal pattern's implied direction or AGAINST it

notes: This is the same TwoBarReversal shape as T06-05/T06-06 but on the opposite side of the trade; deliberately kept as a separate candidate because the entry direction is the mirror of what the raw pattern implies.

candidates.name: ThreeBarReversal
candidates.quote: A three-bar reversal is just a variation of a two-bar reversal where there are three consecutive bars, with the first and third being the bars of a two-bar reversal and the middle bar being an unremarkable bar, like a small bar or a doji.
candidates.description: Primitive: bars 2 and 0 form a two-bar-reversal pair (skipping bar 1), and the skipped middle bar (bar 1) is small relative to recent bars.
candidates.pseudocode: TrendBar[2] (bear) && TrendBar[0] (bull) && (min(high[0],high[2]) - max(low[0],low[2])) >= overlapFraction * min(range(0),range(2)) && body(0) >= bodySizeRatioMin * body(2) && body(0) <= bodySizeRatioMax * body(2) && (high[1] - low[1]) <= middleBarMaxFraction * avgRange(rangeLookback)

complexity.reason: a three-bar shape test reusing TwoBarReversal's ratios plus a small-middle-bar test

candidates.name: ThreeBarReversalEntry
candidates.quote: traders could trade the 5 minute pattern if it was a perfect 15 minute reversal and buy at one tick above the high of the three bars, or earlier if there was an earlier 5 minute entry.
candidates.description: Enter beyond the combined extreme of the three bars forming a three-bar reversal.
candidates.pseudocode: ThreeBarReversal[0]
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop one tick above the highest high of the three bars (or, if the last two bars alone already form a two-bar reversal, one tick above their combined high for an earlier entry)

complexity.reason: inherits ThreeBarReversal

notes: Brooks explicitly says traders should not spend much time hunting for these; they are rare (a couple a day).

candidates.name: IIPattern
candidates.quote: An ii pattern is an inside bar that follows a larger inside bar. It is two in a row with the second being inside the first and of the same size or smaller.
candidates.description: Primitive: two consecutive inside bars, the more recent one inside the one before it (Brooks allows either extreme to be equal, per ch6 p137's inside-bar note).
candidates.pseudocode: (high[0] <= high[1] && low[0] >= low[1]) && (high[1] <= high[2] && low[1] >= low[2])

complexity.reason: two chained two-bar inside comparisons

notes: An 'iii' pattern (three inside bars in a row) is the same test extended one more bar; not split into its own candidate.

candidates.name: IIPatternBreakoutEntry
candidates.quote: traders would buy on a stop at one tick above the second bar.
candidates.description: Enter on a breakout of the ii pattern in the direction of the break; the stop is placed beyond the opposite side of BOTH bars, not just the second (signal) bar.
candidates.pseudocode: IIPattern[0]
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop one tick above max(high[0], high[1]) (long) / sell stop one tick below min(low[0], low[1]) (short); often placed as an OCO bracket in breakout mode, the unfilled side becoming the protective stop

complexity.reason: inherits the trivial IIPattern shape test

candidates.name: IOIPattern
candidates.quote: An ioi pattern, which is an inside bar followed by an outside bar and then another inside bar (inside-outside-inside).
candidates.description: Primitive: bar 2 is an inside bar, bar 1 is an outside bar (relative to bar 2), and bar 0 is an inside bar (relative to bar 1).
candidates.pseudocode: (high[2] <= high[3] && low[2] >= low[3]) && (high[1] >= high[2] && low[1] <= low[2] && (high[1] > high[2] || low[1] < low[2])) && (high[0] <= high[1] && low[0] >= low[1])

complexity.reason: chains an inside-bar test, an outside-bar test, and another inside-bar test

candidates.name: IOIBreakoutEntry
candidates.quote: it is often prudent to place a sell stop below and a buy stop above that second inside bar and enter in the direction of the breakout. The unfilled order then becomes the protective stop.
candidates.description: Enter on the breakout of the second (most recent) inside bar of an ioi pattern, in either direction (breakout mode).
candidates.pseudocode: IOIPattern[0]
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop one tick above high[0] / sell stop one tick below low[0], OCO bracket; the unfilled side becomes the protective stop

complexity.reason: inherits IOIPattern

candidates.name: SmallBarNearBigBarExtreme
candidates.quote: A small bar near the high or low of a big bar (trend bar or outside bar) or trading range (especially if its body is in the direction of your trade, indicating that your side has taken control).
candidates.description: A small-range bar forming near the low of a larger recent bar or swing, closing up (with-trend/fade buy setup showing that buyers have taken control at that level).
candidates.pseudocode: (high[0] - low[0]) <= smallFraction * avgRange(rangeLookback) && low[0] <= lowest(low, bigBarLookback)[1] + nearTicks * tick && close[0] > open[0]
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop one tick above high[0]

complexity.reason: a small-bar test plus proximity to a recent local extreme, both window-based

notes: 'Big bar' here is approximated as the lowest low of a short recent window; Brooks's actual test is visual bar-size comparison, not a specific lookback.

candidates.name: DojiPoorSignalFilter
candidates.quote: Note that doji bars are rarely good signal bars because they are one-bar trading ranges and when the market is in a trading range, you should not be looking to buy above the high or go short below the low.
candidates.description: Context filter: a doji bar (near-zero body relative to its range) is rarely a good signal bar. Brooks allows two exceptions -- a with-trend doji in a strong trend, and a doji at the extreme of a trading range -- but only the with-trend exception is mechanized here; the trading-range-extreme exception needs a trading-range/extreme detector, which this filter does not attempt.
candidates.pseudocode: isDoji = (high[0] - low[0]) > 0 && abs(close[0] - open[0]) <= dojiBodyFraction * (high[0] - low[0]); filter blocks a breakout-of-bar-0 entry when isDoji, unless TrendSpikeContext[0] holds (same direction as the intended trade)

complexity.reason: the doji test itself is trivial, but the book's exceptions (with-trend in a strong trend, or at a trading-range extreme) require the same trend/range judgment calls flagged elsewhere in this file

candidates.name: MicroDoubleExtreme
candidates.quote: A micro double bottom is consecutive or nearly consecutive bars with identical or nearly identical lows.
candidates.description: Primitive: two consecutive bars with matching (within a tick tolerance) lows -- a micro double bottom. Mirrored form: matching highs -- a micro double top.
candidates.pseudocode: abs(low[0] - low[1]) <= matchTicks * tick

complexity.reason: a tolerance comparison of two bars' extremes

notes: 'Nearly consecutive' (a small gap of one or two bars between the matching extremes) is not modeled; only the strict two-consecutive-bar case is covered.

candidates.name: MicroDoubleFlagContinuation
candidates.quote: When it forms in a bear spike and it is a bear trend bar closing on or near its low and then a bull trend bar opening on or near its low, it is a one-bar bear flag. If the lows are identical, consider selling at one tick below the low.
candidates.description: Continuation entry: within a trend spike, a micro double match AGAINST the spike direction (e.g. matching HIGHS during a BULL spike) is read as a one-bar flag, not a reversal -- enter WITH the spike beyond the matched extreme. Long form: matching highs during a bull spike (the mirror image of the book's bear-spike example).
candidates.pseudocode: TrendSpikeContext[0] (bull) && abs(high[0] - high[1]) <= matchTicks * tick
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop one tick above the matched high(s)

complexity.reason: inherits the spike-identification judgment from TrendSpikeContext

notes: Also covers the plain 'two-bar double top/bottom buy/sell setup' described later in the chapter (identical highs/lows in a strong trend used as a with-trend continuation trap), which is the same pattern under a different name.

candidates.name: MicroDoubleReversalEntry
candidates.quote: At all other times, it is more likely a reversal pattern, since most small bull reversals come from some type of micro double bottom.
candidates.description: Reversal entry: OUTSIDE of an opposing spike, a micro double bottom (matching lows) is read as a bullish reversal -- enter long above the pattern's high. Mirror: a micro double top outside a bull spike is a bearish reversal.
candidates.pseudocode: MicroDoubleExtreme[0] (bull form, matching lows) && !TrendSpikeContext[0] (bear)
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop one tick above high[0] (or the higher of the two matching-low bars)

complexity.reason: inherits the spike-identification judgment from TrendSpikeContext

candidates.name: BullReversalBar
candidates.quote: if a trader buys on a stop at one tick above a bull reversal bar that is eight ticks tall, he might put a protective stop at one tick below the bar.
candidates.description: Primitive: bar 0 is a bull reversal bar (a 'good signal bar') -- closes up, close in the upper part of its range, with a lower tail showing rejection of lower prices.
candidates.pseudocode: close[0] > open[0] && (close[0] - low[0]) >= closePositionMin * (high[0] - low[0]) && (open[0] - low[0]) >= lowerTailMin * (high[0] - low[0])

complexity.reason: single-bar arithmetic

notes: Same primitive as T07-03, defined independently here per the one-primitive-per-chapter rule; needed locally for T06-20/21.

candidates.name: ReversalBarFailure
candidates.quote: A reversal bar failure is the bar after a reversal bar that breaks out of the wrong side of the reversal (e.g., if there is a bear reversal bar in a bull trend and the next bar trades above its high instead of below its low).
candidates.description: Primitive event: the bar after a bull reversal bar trades below its low instead of continuing up through its high -- the implied long setup has failed.
candidates.pseudocode: BullReversalBar[1] && low[0] < low[1]

complexity.reason: reversal-bar test plus one comparison on the following bar

candidates.name: ReversalBarFailureFadeEntry
candidates.quote: Perhaps there were early longs who entered on the reversal bar before it triggered a buy signal, and these overly eager bulls were now trapped. They would exit at one tick below the bull reversal bar, which was where smart traders went short.
candidates.description: When a bull reversal bar's implied long fails (price instead breaks below its low), fade it: go short one tick below the failure bar's low, capitalizing on trapped longs exiting there. Mirror: a bear reversal bar failure (price breaks above its high) is a long fade.
candidates.pseudocode: ReversalBarFailure[0] (bear form: BearReversalBar[1] && high[0] > high[1])
candidates.book_order_type: sell stop one tick below low[0]

complexity.reason: inherits ReversalBarFailure

notes: Pages cited are from Figure 6.2's discussion (pp. 144-145 in the running chapter text); the [[page]] markers for that figure use the book's absolute PDF numbering shown in the source file.

candidates.name: ShavedBar
candidates.quote: A shaved bar has no tail at one or both of its extremes.
candidates.description: Primitive: bar 0 has no meaningful tail at its top (closes at or within a tick of its high) -- a shaved top, read as bullish strength. Mirrored form: no tail at the bottom (closes at or within a tick of its low) -- a shaved bottom, read as bearish strength.
candidates.pseudocode: (high[0] - close[0]) <= shaveTicks * tick

complexity.reason: single-bar arithmetic

candidates.name: ShavedBarEntry
candidates.quote: It is a setup only when it forms in a strong trend (e.g., in a strong bull trend, if there is a bull trend bar with no tail on its top or bottom, then it is a buy setup).
candidates.description: In a trend spike, a shaved-top bar (long) / shaved-bottom bar (short) is a with-trend breakout setup.
candidates.pseudocode: ShavedBar[0] && TrendSpikeContext[0]
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop one tick above high[0] (or enter at the market, since the close into the high already shows the strength)

complexity.reason: inherits the spike-identification judgment from TrendSpikeContext

candidates.name: ShavedBarLowVolumeFilter
candidates.quote: When the market is quiet and the volume is low, shaved tops and bottoms are sometimes common and are not a sign of strength... Each of those bars is a trap.
candidates.description: Blocks ShavedBarEntry when several shaved bars have clustered in the recent bars and this bar's volume is below its own average -- a sign of a quiet, low-volume trading range rather than genuine strength.
candidates.pseudocode: countIf(k = 0..clusterLookback-1, ShavedBar[k] (either side)) >= clusterCountMin && volume[0] <= volumeFraction * average(volume, volAvgLookback)

complexity.reason: a windowed count plus a volume-average comparison

notes: Brooks ties this to volume being 'low' without a number; the volume-average test is this pass's reading of that.

candidates.name: ExhaustionBar
candidates.quote: An unusually large trend bar that forms in a trend that has lasted for 10 or more bars usually means that the market is exhausted and will correct for at least 10 bars.
candidates.description: Primitive: an unusually large trend bar (well beyond the recent average range) occurring after an already-established run of same-direction trend bars -- a climactic exhaustion bar.
candidates.pseudocode: TrendBar[0] (bull) && (high[0] - low[0]) >= exhaustionMultiple * avgRange(rangeLookback) && TrendSpikeContext[1] (bull, spikeBars = establishedTrendBars)

complexity.reason: an average-range comparison plus the TrendSpikeContext judgment for 'the trend has lasted 10 or more bars'

candidates.name: ExhaustionCorrectionFilter
candidates.quote: usually means that the market is exhausted and will correct for at least 10 bars, and sometimes it leads to a reversal.
candidates.description: Blocks new with-trend entries for a number of bars after an exhaustion bar, since a correction of at least that many bars is expected.
candidates.pseudocode: filter blocks a with-trend entry when exists k in 0..correctionBars-1 such that ExhaustionBar[k] (same direction as the intended trade)

complexity.reason: a windowed lookback over the ExhaustionBar primitive

candidates.name: Ema20
candidates.quote: if there is a strong bull trend and at least 20 consecutive bars have been above the moving average, and the market drifts sideways to the rising moving average, look to buy the close of the first small bear trend bar.
candidates.description: Primitive: the 20-bar exponential moving average of closes; 'above the EMA' = close[0] > ema[0].
candidates.pseudocode: ema = XAverage(close, emaLength); close[0] > ema[0]

complexity.reason: needs an EMA state variable

notes: Same primitive as T07-06, defined independently here per the one-primitive-per-chapter rule.

candidates.name: ConsecutiveBarsBeyondEma
candidates.quote: at least 20 consecutive bars have been above the moving average
candidates.description: Context filter: the last establishedBars bars all closed above (bull) / below (bear) the 20-bar EMA -- an established with-trend run.
candidates.pseudocode: for k in 0..establishedBars-1: close[k] > ema[k] -> allAboveEma; filter passes when allAboveEma

complexity.reason: a 20-bar window over an EMA state variable

candidates.name: MovingAverageGapBarPullbackEntry
candidates.quote: look to buy the close of the first small bear trend bar with a close that is only a tick or two below the moving average. Also, look to buy above its high.
candidates.description: After an established bull run (bars closing above the EMA for a while), buy the close of the first small counter-colored (bear) trend bar that closes within a tick or two of the EMA -- a with-trend continuation entry on the pullback's exhaustion.
candidates.pseudocode: ConsecutiveBarsBeyondEma[1] (bull) && TrendBar[0] (bear) && abs(close[0] - ema[0]) <= gapTicks * tick
candidates.book_order_type: buy at the market on the bar's close, and also place a buy stop one tick above its high

complexity.reason: combines the EMA state variable with a small counter-colored-bar test

notes: This is the '20 gap bar' setup Brooks refers to repeatedly through the chapter's chart discussions (e.g. pp. 142-143, 165); the general EMA-gap-bar idea is also referenced from T07-06/T07-08.

candidates.name: AllBarsInChannelLimitEntry
candidates.quote: When there is a strong bull channel, bulls will place limit orders to buy at or below the low of the prior bar, and bears will place limit orders to short at or above the high of every bar.
candidates.description: In a strong bull channel (approximated here by the same sustained-trend proxy as TrendSpikeContext, extended over more bars), buy at or below the prior bar's low with a resting limit order. Mirror: in a bear channel, sell at or above the prior bar's high.
candidates.pseudocode: TrendSpikeContext[0] (bull, spikeBars = channelBars) && low[0] <= low[1]
candidates.book_order_type: resting buy limit order at or below the prior bar's low, working continuously while the channel context holds -- not a stop; assumes a fill at low[1] on this bar rather than the usual next-bar-open mechanization, since a limit order can fill intrabar

complexity.reason: channel is approximated by the sustained-trend-bar proxy already used for TrendSpikeContext; the intrabar limit fill is also an exception to the standard close-then-next-open mechanization and would need explicit engine support

notes: 'Channel' is a chart-pattern concept (a shallow, sustained trend with small pullbacks) that Brooks develops fully elsewhere in the trilogy; not re-derived from scratch here.

candidates.name: SecondEntryPreferenceFilter
candidates.quote: Second entries in general are more reliable.
candidates.description: Context filter, repeated throughout the chapter: prefer the second occurrence of a given setup type over the first, since the first attempt after a strong move often fails. Recorded as a research-grade placeholder because 'the same setup type' and 'failed' are not primitives this engine currently tracks per placement.
candidates.pseudocode: filter passes only when this Entry candidate's pattern also fired (and did not trigger, or triggered and reversed within failedWithinBars bars) at least once in the last lookbackBars bars on the same side

complexity.reason: needs a per-placement 'did this same Entry candidate recently fire and fail' counter, which is not an existing engine primitive; 'the same setup' and 'failed' both need a design decision

notes: Stated so often in this chapter (and the rest of the trilogy) that it is worth flagging even though it cannot be mechanized cleanly without new engine support.

candidates.name: MiddayDojiFilter
candidates.quote: that is when the bar is a small doji (small relative to the recent bars), especially if it has no body, it is near the moving average, and it occurs approximately between 10:00 a.m. and 11:00 a.m. PST. These have a very high failure rate.
candidates.description: Blocks a doji-based signal bar (see DojiPoorSignalFilter) that also falls within a specific time-of-day window and is near a flat moving average -- an even weaker subset of the general doji-filter case, intraday only.
candidates.pseudocode: isDoji (as in T06-15) && abs(close[0] - ema[0]) <= flatEmaTicks * tick && ctx.Time() >= windowStart && ctx.Time() <= windowEnd

complexity.reason: combines the doji test with a time-window check and a proximity-to-EMA check

notes: Time window is stated in PST; the engine's ctx.Time() is exchange-clock, matching the corpus's existing TimeWindow/TimeOfDayExit convention.

rejected.quote: you will be able to find one where the setup actually is a perfect two-bar reversal... on some higher time frame chart
rejected.reason: requires a bar series from a different timeframe than the one being traded, which this engine does not have

rejected.quote: However, a trader would have to think quickly to realize this and place an order.
rejected.reason: pure discretion about execution speed, no bar-level test

rejected.quote: However, there will always be a successful breakout eventually.
rejected.reason: not a decidable bar-level condition -- an eventual-certainty statement with no defined trigger

rejected.quote: bar 1 was a Hammer doji bar... even though it was a double bottom with the first bar of the day, this was a bad setup for price action traders
rejected.reason: a specific chart narrative illustrating already-recorded general concepts (doji, trading range, moving-average test), not itself a new statable rule

chapter_summary: Chapter 6 catalogs signal-bar types beyond the plain trend bar and reversal bar covered elsewhere: strong trend bars entered at the close, two- and three-bar reversals (and the counter-reading where a strong trend fades the reversal instead), small-bar families (ii/iii, ioi, small-bar-near-a-big-bar-extreme), doji caveats (generally poor signal bars, with with-trend and time-of-day exceptions), micro double tops/bottoms (read as continuation flags inside a spike or as reversals outside one), reversal bar failure (trapped-trader fades), shaved bars (strength in a trend, meaningless clustering in a quiet range), exhaustion bars (large trend bars after 10+ bars implying a correction), the moving-average-gap-bar pullback entry, and channel-style resting limit orders. Most candidates lean on two chapter-local context primitives -- TrendSpikeContext (short-window, spike-phase proxy) and ConsecutiveBarsBeyondEma (longer-window, established-trend proxy) -- reused across many candidates with different lookback parameters rather than re-derived per pattern; the dedup pass should treat these as the chapter's two 'trend-strength' primitives alongside T07-08's independent StrongTrendContext. The bulk of the chapter's raw text is per-chart 'Deeper Discussion' narrative (specific bar numbers on specific figures) illustrating wedges, measured moves, climaxes, and trend-channel-line overshoots; those concepts are not this chapter's subject and are deliberately not re-mined here to avoid shadow-defining primitives that belong to the trilogy's dedicated chapters on trend lines, channels, and reversals (book 3). About ten pages in the middle of the chapter's PDF extraction lost inter-word spacing (e.g. the 'Deeper Discussion' block around p.152-153); they were read in full but contained only narrative, no new rule content.
